n-m-e2-s1-01.title: How Many Lockers Are Between the Numbers?
n-m-e2-s1-01.topic: Three-digit numbers: how many numbers are between two numbers
n-m-e2-s1-01.goal: Learn that the difference of two numbers and the count of numbers between them can be different, and tell that the count changes depending on whether the two ends are included.
n-m-e2-s1-01.material: The school lockers are numbered from 305 to 310. Doyun wants to find out how many lockers are between them, not counting lockers 305 and 310. Doyun wrote the solution like this.
n-m-e2-s1-01.thinking.0: Find the first wrong place in a solution
n-m-e2-s1-01.thinking.1: Decide the boundary of whether to include or leave out the two ends
n-m-e2-s1-01.thinking.2: Count by hand and compare with the subtraction result
n-m-e2-s1-01.prereq.0: Knowing the order and size of three-digit numbers
n-m-e2-s1-01.s.s1.prompt: Choose the one line in Doyun's solution that is wrong for the first time.
n-m-e2-s1-01.s.s1.hint.0: Point at the numbers Doyun wrote on line 1 one by one with your finger, and count how many there are in all.
n-m-e2-s1-01.s.s1.hint.1: For each line, compare the number Doyun said with the result you counted by hand earlier. Find the first line that does not match.
n-m-e2-s1-01.s.s1.line.0: I wrote out all the numbers: 305, 306, 307, 308, 309, 310.
n-m-e2-s1-01.s.s1.line.1: 310 − 305 = 5, so there are 5 of these numbers in all.
n-m-e2-s1-01.s.s1.line.2: Lockers 305 and 310 must be left out, so I subtract 2 from 5.
n-m-e2-s1-01.s.s1.line.3: So there are 3 lockers in between.
n-m-e2-s1-01.s.s1.explain: Line 1 is correct. If you count the numbers Doyun wrote on line 2, there are 6 from 305 to 310. 310 − 305 = 5 is the number of steps from one number to the next, not the count of numbers. The method on line 3 (leaving out the two numbers) is fine, but it carried on the 5 from line 2, so the answer on line 4 is wrong. The first wrong place is line 2.
n-m-e2-s1-01.s.s2.prompt: Make two different cases where there are exactly 7 lockers between two numbers, not counting those two numbers. Choose a start number a and an end number b. The locker numbers are all three-digit numbers.
n-m-e2-s1-01.s.s2.hint.0: Choose a start number, and write 7 numbers in order starting with the number after it.
n-m-e2-s1-01.s.s2.hint.1: The number after the 7 you wrote is the end number. Compare the start number and the end number.
n-m-e2-s1-01.s.s2.fail.c1: Please make a a number from 100 to 999.
n-m-e2-s1-01.s.s2.fail.c2: Please make b a number from 100 to 999.
n-m-e2-s1-01.s.s2.fail.c3: The start number a must be less than the end number b.
n-m-e2-s1-01.s.s2.ok.c4: There are 7 numbers between number a and number b.
n-m-e2-s1-01.s.s2.fail.c4: Leave out a and b, and write the numbers between them one by one and count. Are there 7?
n-m-e2-s1-01.s.s2.explain: If there are 7 numbers between a and b, then b is 8 more than a. If you leave out both end numbers when counting, you get 1 fewer than b − a.
n-m-e2-s1-01.s.s3.prompt: Dooyoon wrote 310 − 305 = 5. In which way of counting the numbers is this the right count?
n-m-e2-s1-01.s.s3.hint.0: Write out the numbers from 305 to 310, and count them in different ways to see how many there are each time.
n-m-e2-s1-01.s.s3.hint.1: Compare how the count changes when you include the end numbers and when you leave them out.
n-m-e2-s1-01.s.s3.o.a: Counting with both number 305 and number 310 included
n-m-e2-s1-01.s.s3.r.a: If you include both, you get 305, 306, 307, 308, 309, 310, which is 6.
n-m-e2-s1-01.s.s3.o.b: Counting with both number 305 and number 310 left out
n-m-e2-s1-01.s.s3.r.b: If you leave out both, you get 306, 307, 308, 309, which is 4.
n-m-e2-s1-01.s.s3.o.c: Counting with only one end number included and the other left out
n-m-e2-s1-01.s.s3.r.c: If you include 305 and leave out 310, you get 305 to 309, which is 5. It is also 5 the other way around.
n-m-e2-s1-01.s.s3.o.d: No matter how you count, it is always 5
n-m-e2-s1-01.s.s3.r.d: The count changes depending on how you count. Write the numbers out and count them yourself.
n-m-e2-s1-01.s.s3.explain: Including both numbers gives 6, leaving out both gives 4, and including only one gives 5. Subtraction tells you the "number of steps between", so you need to decide which numbers you are counting and then add or subtract one.

n-m-e2-s1-02.title: Will Four Sticks Always Make a Quadrilateral?
n-m-e2-s1-02.topic: Shapes: Conditions for Making a Quadrilateral
n-m-e2-s1-02.goal: Learners see that having 4 straight lines is not enough to make a quadrilateral, and revise their thinking as they get more information: the ends must connect with no gaps and the lines must not cross.
n-m-e2-s1-02.material: Harin is playing with 4 straight sticks. She wants to make a quadrilateral with the sticks. A quadrilateral is a shape enclosed by 4 straight lines.
n-m-e2-s1-02.thinking.1: Changing your judgment to fit new information
n-m-e2-s1-02.thinking.2: Sorting out what does not matter for the shape (length, right angles)
n-m-e2-s1-02.prereq.0: Knowing triangles and quadrilaterals (shapes enclosed by straight lines)
n-m-e2-s1-02.s.s1.prompt: Choose how your thinking changes each time new information appears.
n-m-e2-s1-02.s.s1.hint.0: Draw the sticks on paper, and redraw how the sticks are placed each time new information appears.
n-m-e2-s1-02.s.s1.hint.1: At each step, check whether all the lines around the shape are connected and whether any lines cross.
n-m-e2-s1-02.s.s1.st.0.info: Harin put 4 straight sticks on the desk. We do not know yet how the sticks are placed relative to each other.
n-m-e2-s1-02.s.s1.st.0.ask: With 4 sticks, can we say it has become a quadrilateral?
n-m-e2-s1-02.s.s1.st.0.after: Just having 4 sticks does not tell us whether it is a quadrilateral. We also need to know how the ends of the sticks are placed.
n-m-e2-s1-02.s.s1.st.0.o.a: Yes, there are 4 sticks, so it is a quadrilateral
n-m-e2-s1-02.s.s1.st.0.r.a: This thinking looks only at the number of sticks. You also need to look at how the sticks are placed.
n-m-e2-s1-02.s.s1.st.0.o.b: We need to know more about how the sticks are placed
n-m-e2-s1-02.s.s1.st.0.r.b: This thinking looks at the way the sticks are placed, not just how many there are.
n-m-e2-s1-02.s.s1.st.0.o.c: No, you cannot make a quadrilateral with sticks
n-m-e2-s1-02.s.s1.st.0.r.c: You can make a quadrilateral with 4 straight sticks.
n-m-e2-s1-02.s.s1.st.0.o.d: If all the sticks are the same length, it is a quadrilateral
n-m-e2-s1-02.s.s1.st.0.r.d: Even if the lengths are the same, if the sticks are placed apart from each other, they do not make an enclosed shape.
n-m-e2-s1-02.s.s1.st.1.info: Harin connected the ends of the sticks and went all the way around. There are no gaps between the sticks, and no places where the sticks overlap or cross.
n-m-e2-s1-02.s.s1.st.1.ask: Can we say it is a quadrilateral now?
n-m-e2-s1-02.s.s1.st.1.after: When 4 straight lines go all the way around with no gaps, we can say it is a quadrilateral. Is that still true if the sticks are placed in a different shape?
n-m-e2-s1-02.s.s1.st.1.o.a: No, the corners must be right angles for it to be a quadrilateral
n-m-e2-s1-02.s.s1.st.1.r.a: Even without right angles, a shape enclosed by 4 straight lines is a quadrilateral.
n-m-e2-s1-02.s.s1.st.1.o.b: Not yet, we need to connect more sticks
n-m-e2-s1-02.s.s1.st.1.r.b: It already goes all the way around with no gaps. No more sticks are needed.
n-m-e2-s1-02.s.s1.st.1.o.c: Yes, it is enclosed by 4 straight lines, so it is a quadrilateral
n-m-e2-s1-02.s.s1.st.1.r.c: You thought in line with the meaning that a quadrilateral is a shape enclosed by 4 straight lines.
n-m-e2-s1-02.s.s1.st.1.o.d: No, the sticks must all be the same length for it to be a quadrilateral
n-m-e2-s1-02.s.s1.st.1.r.d: It can be a quadrilateral even if the lengths are different.
n-m-e2-s1-02.s.s1.st.2.info: Harin made a new shape. The ends of all four sticks are connected with no gaps. The left stick and the right stick are standing upright. One slanted stick goes from the upper left to the lower right, and the other goes from the lower left to the upper right, so the two sticks cross each other in the middle in an X shape.
n-m-e2-s1-02.s.s1.st.2.ask: What shapes can you see inside this shape?
n-m-e2-s1-02.s.s1.st.2.after: Even if 4 sticks are connected with no gaps, if they cross in the middle, two triangles are made. In this task, we will not count a shape like this as a quadrilateral.
n-m-e2-s1-02.s.s1.st.2.r.a: You cannot see a quadrilateral inside. Look at the pieces divided around the center point.
n-m-e2-s1-02.s.s1.st.2.r.b: If the sticks cross in the middle, it is not a single quadrilateral shape.
n-m-e2-s1-02.s.s1.st.2.r.c: You can see pieces enclosed by straight lines.
n-m-e2-s1-02.s.s1.st.2.r.d: The left piece and the right piece that meet at the center point are each a triangle.
n-m-e2-s1-02.s.s1.reflect: At first you only knew there were 4 sticks, next you learned how the sticks were connected, and finally you learned about the case where they cross. Tell which step changed your thinking and what you need to check for it to be a quadrilateral.
n-m-e2-s1-02.s.s2.prompt: Choose everything you must follow when making a quadrilateral with 4 sticks.
n-m-e2-s1-02.s.s2.hint.0: In the three steps, find the shapes that are quadrilaterals and the ones that are not, and compare them.
n-m-e2-s1-02.s.s2.hint.1: Try each sentence on another shape that is a quadrilateral (a quadrilateral with different lengths) and check whether that shape is still a quadrilateral.
n-m-e2-s1-02.s.s2.o.a: You must make all four sticks the same length
n-m-e2-s1-02.s.s2.r.a: It is a quadrilateral even if the lengths are different. The lengths do not have to be the same.
n-m-e2-s1-02.s.s2.o.b: The ends of the sticks must connect with no gaps and go all the way around
n-m-e2-s1-02.s.s2.r.b: If the ends are not connected, the sticks do not make an enclosed shape.
n-m-e2-s1-02.s.s2.o.c: All four corners must be right angles
n-m-e2-s1-02.s.s2.r.c: It is a quadrilateral even if the corners are not right angles.
n-m-e2-s1-02.s.s2.o.d: The sticks must be placed so that they do not cross in the middle
n-m-e2-s1-02.s.s2.r.d: If they cross, the shape is divided into two triangles.
n-m-e2-s1-02.s.s2.explain: To be a quadrilateral, the ends of the sticks must connect with no gaps and go all the way around, and the sticks must not cross. Equal lengths or right angles are only some of the many kinds of quadrilaterals.
n-m-e2-s1-02.s.s3.prompt: Your younger sibling says, "If you have just 4 straight sticks, you get a quadrilateral." Write one reason to tell your sibling why this is not always true.
n-m-e2-s1-02.s.s3.hint.0: Think of one stick arrangement from above that did not make a quadrilateral, and describe it in words as if drawing a picture.
n-m-e2-s1-02.s.s3.hint.1: Look at how the ends of the sticks are placed and whether the sticks cross, and write about it.
n-m-e2-s1-02.s.s3.placeholder: Example: If the ends of the sticks ...
n-m-e2-s1-02.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you say at least one thing that 4 sticks alone are missing?
n-m-e2-s1-02.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you give an example of how the sticks are placed (ends apart, crossing)?
n-m-e2-s1-02.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you write in simple words so your younger sibling can understand?
n-m-e2-s1-02.s.s3.model.0: If the ends of the sticks are not connected and are apart, the shape is not enclosed, so it is not a quadrilateral.
n-m-e2-s1-02.s.s3.model.1: If you place 4 sticks so they cross in the middle in an X shape, two triangles are made, so it is not a quadrilateral.
n-m-e2-s1-02.s.s3.model.2: Even with 4 sticks, if there is a gap in one place, it is not a closed shape, so you cannot call it a quadrilateral.
n-m-e2-s1-02.s.s3.modelNote.2: I called the case where the ends are not connected "having a gap."
n-m-e2-s1-02.s.s3.model.3: If you lay the sticks on top of each other or place them so the ends do not meet, a quadrilateral is not made.
n-m-e2-s1-02.s.s3.model.4: If you connect four sticks in one long line, it is not a quadrilateral but a long line.

n-m-e2-s1-03.title: Making an Addition with Two Carries
n-m-e2-s1-03.topic: Addition and Subtraction: Addition with Two Carries
n-m-e2-s1-03.goal: Learners work out the conditions for carrying by following the carry from the ones place to the tens place, and see that because of the carried 1, a carry happens even when the sum in the tens place is only 9.
n-m-e2-s1-03.material: Haeun is playing a game of adding two 3-digit numbers. She wants a carry in the ones place and also a carry in the tens place. She wants the sum to be a 3-digit number.
n-m-e2-s1-03.thinking.0: Making several examples yourself that meet the conditions
n-m-e2-s1-03.thinking.1: Finding the hidden condition that the carried number must also be added
n-m-e2-s1-03.thinking.2: Gathering examples and stating the rule
n-m-e2-s1-03.prereq.0: Knowing addition of 3-digit numbers with carrying
n-m-e2-s1-03.s.s1.prompt: We want to find additions where a carry happens in both the ones place and the tens place. Which addition has two carries?
n-m-e2-s1-03.s.s1.hint.0: Write each addition vertically and calculate step by step starting from the ones place.
n-m-e2-s1-03.s.s1.hint.1: Check whether you included the 1 carried from the ones place in the tens place calculation.
n-m-e2-s1-03.s.s1.r.a: In the ones place, 6+8=14 has a carry. In the tens place, 3+5 plus the carried 1 is 9. There is only one carry.
n-m-e2-s1-03.s.s1.r.b: In the ones place, 5+8=13 has a carry, and in the tens place, 7+6 plus the carried 1 is 14, which also has a carry.
n-m-e2-s1-03.s.s1.r.c: In the ones place, 2+5=7 has no carry. A carry happens only once, in the tens place.
n-m-e2-s1-03.s.s1.r.d: In the ones place, 9+7=16 has a carry. In the tens place, 4+3 plus the carried 1 is 8. There is only one carry.
n-m-e2-s1-03.s.s1.explain: 175 + 168 has a carry once in the ones place and once in the tens place, giving 343. The others have only one carry. In the tens place, you must also add the carried 1.
n-m-e2-s1-03.s.s2.prompt: Make three different additions where a carry happens in both the ones place and the tens place, and the sum is a 3-digit number (less than 1000). The two numbers to add, a and b, are 3-digit numbers.
n-m-e2-s1-03.s.s2.hint.0: First choose the two digits in the ones place so that their sum is more than 10.
n-m-e2-s1-03.s.s2.hint.1: Choose the two digits in the tens place, and check whether the sum with the carried 1 added is more than 10.
n-m-e2-s1-03.s.s2.fail.c1: Please choose a from the numbers 100 to 999.
n-m-e2-s1-03.s.s2.fail.c2: Please choose b from the numbers 100 to 999.
n-m-e2-s1-03.s.s2.ok.c3: A carry happens in the ones place.
n-m-e2-s1-03.s.s2.fail.c3: Add the two digits in the ones place. Does a carry happen?
n-m-e2-s1-03.s.s2.ok.c4: A carry also happens in the tens place.
n-m-e2-s1-03.s.s2.fail.c4: Calculate the tens place. Add the carried 1 too. Does a carry happen?
n-m-e2-s1-03.s.s2.fail.c5: The sum must be less than 1000.
n-m-e2-s1-03.s.s2.explain: When a carry happens in the ones place, you add the carried 1 in the tens place. So a carry happens even when the sum of the two digits in the tens place is only 9.
n-m-e2-s1-03.s.s3.prompt: A carry happened in the ones place. For a carry to also happen in the tens place, what must the sum of the two digits in the tens place be at least?
n-m-e2-s1-03.s.s3.hint.0: Change the sum of the two tens digits to 8, 9, and 10, and calculate the value after adding the carried 1.
n-m-e2-s1-03.s.s3.hint.1: Among the additions you made earlier, find the one with the smallest sum in the tens place.
n-m-e2-s1-03.s.s3.o.a: It needs to be 10 or more
n-m-e2-s1-03.s.s3.r.a: This thinking missed adding the carried 1. Even if the sum is only 9, adding the carried 1 makes 10.
n-m-e2-s1-03.s.s3.o.b: It needs to be 8 or more
n-m-e2-s1-03.s.s3.r.b: 8 plus the carried 1 is 9. A carry does not happen.
n-m-e2-s1-03.s.s3.o.c: It needs to be 11 or more
n-m-e2-s1-03.s.s3.r.c: This thinking missed that a carry also happens when the sum is 10.
n-m-e2-s1-03.s.s3.o.d: It needs to be 9 or more
n-m-e2-s1-03.s.s3.r.d: 9 plus the carried 1 makes 10, so a carry happens.
n-m-e2-s1-03.s.s3.explain: In the tens place, a carry happens if the sum of the two digits plus the carried 1 is 10 or more. So the sum of the two digits needs to be 9 or more.

n-m-e2-s1-04.title: Making Lots of Subtractions with a Difference of 148
n-m-e2-s1-04.topic: Addition and Subtraction: Subtractions with the Same Difference
n-m-e2-s1-04.goal: Learners see that the difference stays the same when both numbers change by the same amount, and make several subtractions with a given difference on their own and explain the method.
n-m-e2-s1-04.material: Minseo wants to make lots of subtractions with a difference of 148. She makes ones like 327 − 179 = 148 that need borrowing in the ones place. Minseo is calculating each one to check it.
n-m-e2-s1-04.thinking.1: Finding cases where the distance (difference) between two numbers does not change
n-m-e2-s1-04.prereq.0: Knowing subtraction of 3-digit numbers with borrowing
n-m-e2-s1-04.prereq.1: Thinking about the distance between two numbers on a number line
n-m-e2-s1-04.s.s1.prompt: 327 − 179 = 148. If you add 100 to both 327 and 179 and calculate 427 − 279, what happens to the difference? Make a guess before you calculate.
n-m-e2-s1-04.s.s1.hint.0: Mark 327 and 179 on a number line and measure the distance between them.
n-m-e2-s1-04.s.s1.hint.1: Draw a picture where both numbers move 100 steps to the right, and compare the distance before and after moving.
n-m-e2-s1-04.s.s1.o.a: It gets 100 bigger, so it is 248
n-m-e2-s1-04.s.s1.r.a: Both numbers got 100 bigger, so the difference does not change. Did you think that only one number got bigger?
n-m-e2-s1-04.s.s1.r.b: The two numbers move together by the same amount, so the distance between them stays the same.
n-m-e2-s1-04.s.s1.o.c: It gets 100 smaller, so it is 48
n-m-e2-s1-04.s.s1.r.c: You made both numbers bigger but thought the difference gets smaller. Try drawing a picture.
n-m-e2-s1-04.s.s1.o.d: You cannot tell. You have to calculate
n-m-e2-s1-04.s.s1.r.d: You can tell without calculating. If both numbers move by the same amount, the distance between them stays the same.
n-m-e2-s1-04.s.s1.explain: 427 − 279 = 148. If you add 100 to both numbers, the distance between them stays the same, so the difference stays the same too.
n-m-e2-s1-04.s.s2.prompt: Make three different subtractions with a difference of 148. Subtract the smaller number b from the larger number a. Both numbers are 3-digit numbers, and the ones place must need borrowing.
n-m-e2-s1-04.s.s2.hint.0: Think about whether you can use the given subtraction 327 − 179 to make a new one.
n-m-e2-s1-04.s.s2.hint.1: Decide how to change the two numbers, calculate, and check each time that the difference is 148.
n-m-e2-s1-04.s.s2.fail.c1: Please choose a from the numbers 100 to 999.
n-m-e2-s1-04.s.s2.fail.c2: Please choose b from the numbers 100 to 999.
n-m-e2-s1-04.s.s2.fail.c3: a minus b is not 148. Calculate again.
n-m-e2-s1-04.s.s2.fail.c4: You cannot subtract the ones digits, so you have to borrow from the tens place. Compare the digits in the ones place.
n-m-e2-s1-04.s.s2.explain: If you increase or decrease both numbers in the subtraction you made earlier by the same amount, you can keep making new subtractions with a difference of 148.
n-m-e2-s1-04.s.s3.prompt: So that your partner can also make subtractions with a difference of 148, write with numbers how to change the two numbers so that the difference stays the same.
n-m-e2-s1-04.s.s3.hint.0: Put two of the subtractions you made side by side and compare how the larger numbers and the smaller numbers changed.
n-m-e2-s1-04.s.s3.hint.1: Calculate the difference of your new subtraction yourself and check that it is 148.
n-m-e2-s1-04.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you write that both numbers change by the same amount?
n-m-e2-s1-04.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you check with your own numbers that the difference of the new subtraction is 148?
n-m-e2-s1-04.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you say why the difference stays the same?
n-m-e2-s1-04.s.s3.model.0: If you add 100 to both numbers in 327 − 179, you get 427 − 279. If you increase both by the same amount, the difference stays 148.
n-m-e2-s1-04.s.s3.model.1: Add the same number to the larger number and the smaller number. For example, if you add 3 to both 327 and 179, you get 330 − 182, and the difference is 148.
n-m-e2-s1-04.s.s3.model.2: Subtract 50 from both numbers. 327 − 179 becomes 277 − 129, and the difference stays 148.
n-m-e2-s1-04.s.s3.modelNote.2: I used subtracting instead of adding.
n-m-e2-s1-04.s.s3.model.3: Choose any smaller number and add 148 to make the larger number. For example, 191 plus 148 is 339, and 339 − 191 = 148.
n-m-e2-s1-04.s.s3.modelNote.3: Instead of changing both by the same amount, I used the method of adding 148 to the smaller number.
n-m-e2-s1-04.s.s3.model.4: Just add 3 to both. 327 − 179 becomes 330 − 182, and the difference stays 148.

n-m-e2-s1-05.title: How Should I Describe It So My Friend Guesses the Pentagon Card?
n-m-e2-s1-05.topic: Shapes: Describing with the Number of Sides and Vertices
n-m-e2-s1-05.goal: Learners change words that fit many shapes, like pointy and straight, into numbers of sides or vertices, and rewrite their description so the listening friend can choose just one shape.
n-m-e2-s1-05.material: Soeun is playing a shape card guessing game with a friend. On the desk there is one card each of a triangle, quadrilateral, pentagon, hexagon, and circle. Soeun secretly picks one pentagon card. Her friend picks a card based only on what Soeun says. Soeun first said this: "It has straight lines and it has pointy places."
n-m-e2-s1-05.thinking.0: Rewording so the listener is not confused
n-m-e2-s1-05.thinking.1: Finding the relationship between the number of sides and the number of vertices
n-m-e2-s1-05.thinking.2: Sorting out words that fit many shapes
n-m-e2-s1-05.prereq.0: Knowing the sides and vertices of triangles, quadrilaterals, pentagons, and hexagons
n-m-e2-s1-05.s.s1.prompt: The card Soeun picked is the pentagon. For her friend to choose just the pentagon card, what should Soeun add?
n-m-e2-s1-05.s.s1.hint.0: First write the number of sides and the number of vertices of the five cards in a table.

n-m-e2-s1b-01.title: The Desk Length Jiwoo Estimated
n-m-e2-s1b-01.topic: Measuring Length: Estimating Length in cm and m
n-m-e2-s1b-01.goal: Learners use the length of one hand span to estimate, find where the mistake is when converting between cm and m, and check that an estimated length makes sense by comparing it with 1 m.
n-m-e2-s1b-01.material: Jiwoo knows that her hand span is about 15 cm. She measured the long side of the desk with her hand span and it was 6 spans. With this, Jiwoo estimated the length of the long side of the desk. 1 m is 100 cm. Below is what Jiwoo said, in order.
n-m-e2-s1b-01.thinking.0: Knowing that even if the calculation is right, the mistake can be in the line where the unit is changed
n-m-e2-s1b-01.thinking.1: Checking whether an estimate makes sense by comparing it with 1 m (100 cm)
n-m-e2-s1b-01.prereq.1: Estimating length with hand spans, without a ruler
n-m-e2-s1b-01.s.s1.prompt: Choose the first line that is wrong in Jiwoo's explanation.
n-m-e2-s1b-01.s.s1.hint.0: Redo the calculation of each line yourself and look at which line the unit changes.
n-m-e2-s1b-01.s.s1.hint.1: Take 1 m as 100 cm, and put the lengths up to line 3 in the same unit to compare them.
n-m-e2-s1b-01.s.s1.line.0: Jiwoo's hand span is about 15 cm.
n-m-e2-s1b-01.s.s1.line.1: The long side of the desk is 6 spans, so add 15 six times. 15+15+15+15+15+15=90.
n-m-e2-s1b-01.s.s1.line.2: 90 cm is the same as 9 m.
n-m-e2-s1b-01.s.s1.line.3: So the long side of the desk is about 9 m.
n-m-e2-s1b-01.s.s1.explain: Line 1 and line 2 are right. Adding 15 six times gives 90, and the unit stays cm. In line 3, 90 cm was called 9 m, but 1 m is 100 cm, so 90 cm is a little shorter than 1 m. Line 4 carries on from the wrong line 3. Written correctly, the long side of the desk is about 90 cm.
n-m-e2-s1b-01.s.s2.prompt: What is the best way to check that an estimated length makes sense?
n-m-e2-s1b-01.s.s2.hint.0: Think about whether the length of the long side of the desk fits better next to your height or the height of the classroom door.
n-m-e2-s1b-01.s.s2.hint.1: Choose one length you know well, and compare whether the estimate is shorter or longer than that length.
n-m-e2-s1b-01.s.s2.o.a: Add or remove one zero from the estimated number.
n-m-e2-s1b-01.s.s2.r.a: There is no reason for adding or removing a zero. Changing only the number does not check the relationship between units.
n-m-e2-s1b-01.s.s2.o.b: Calculate once more in the same way.
n-m-e2-s1b-01.s.s2.r.b: If you redo it the same way, you will make the same mistake in the same place. The calculation was right; the problem was where the unit was changed.
n-m-e2-s1b-01.s.s2.o.c: Compare the estimated length with a length you know well.
n-m-e2-s1b-01.s.s2.o.d: Ask a friend whether they say the same number.
n-m-e2-s1b-01.s.s2.r.d: Even if a friend says the same thing, that does not guarantee it is right. You need to compare with a reference length.
n-m-e2-s1b-01.s.s2.explain: If you compare the estimated length with a length you know well, like 1 m (100 cm), you can tell which of 90 cm and 9 m fits the desk. 9 m is even longer than one wall of the classroom.
n-m-e2-s1b-01.s.s3.prompt: Compare the length of the long side of the desk with 1 m to write a correct estimate, and write in one sentence what to fix in Jiwoo's statement.
n-m-e2-s1b-01.s.s3.hint.0: First decide whether the desk is longer or shorter than 1 m.
n-m-e2-s1b-01.s.s3.hint.1: Write how many cm 1 m is, and compare it with 90 cm.
n-m-e2-s1b-01.s.s3.placeholder: Example: The long side of the desk is about ... Jiwoo ...
n-m-e2-s1b-01.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you write the estimated length with its unit?
n-m-e2-s1b-01.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you use the fact that 1 m is 100 cm to say what to fix?
n-m-e2-s1b-01.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you write it so Jiwoo can easily understand?
n-m-e2-s1b-01.s.s3.model.0: The long side of the desk is about 90 cm. 90 cm is shorter than 1 m (100 cm), so it is not 9 m.
n-m-e2-s1b-01.s.s3.model.1: It is about 90 cm. Jiwoo wrongly changed 90 cm into 9 m. Since 1 m is 100 cm, 90 cm is a little shorter than 1 m.
n-m-e2-s1b-01.s.s3.model.2: The desk is about 90 centimeters, close to 1 m. You need to fix the place where you changed it to 9 m.
n-m-e2-s1b-01.s.s3.model.3: The desk is about 90 cm, a little shorter than 1 m. Jiwoo needs to fix the place where she called 90 cm 9 m.
n-m-e2-s1b-01.s.s3.model.4: The long side of the desk is about 1 m. Jiwoo changed the unit wrongly.

n-m-e2-s1b-02.title: Making 1 m Without a Ruler
n-m-e2-s1b-02.topic: Measuring Length: Estimating 1 m by Laying Objects of Known Length End to End
n-m-e2-s1b-02.goal: Learners decide on a way to estimate a length close to 1 m (100 cm) by laying objects of known length end to end, make several combinations themselves, and think about which way the estimate is off when gaps appear while laying them end to end.
n-m-e2-s1b-02.material: Jia wants to tie a 1 m long ribbon around a gift box. 1 m is 100 cm. There is no long ruler at home, only small objects whose lengths she knows. Jia wants to lay objects of the same kind in a line end to end to estimate about 1 m.
n-m-e2-s1b-02.thinking.0: Setting a reference length and estimating by repeating it
n-m-e2-s1b-02.thinking.1: Making the same estimate with several different combinations
n-m-e2-s1b-02.thinking.2: Thinking about which direction an estimate is off
n-m-e2-s1b-02.prereq.2: Adding the same number several times (multiplication)
n-m-e2-s1b-02.s.s1.prompt: What is the most reliable way to estimate about 1 m without a ruler?
n-m-e2-s1b-02.s.s1.hint.0: Think about what you need to know in order to tell another person the estimated length.
n-m-e2-s1b-02.s.s1.hint.1: Think about how you can find the total length from two things: the length of one object and the number of times you laid it down.
n-m-e2-s1b-02.s.s1.o.a: Take one quick look and decide the length by feeling.
n-m-e2-s1b-02.s.s1.r.a: Feelings alone make big differences between people. You need a reference of known length to be reliable.
n-m-e2-s1b-02.s.s1.o.b: Lay various objects end to end however you like, without knowing their lengths.
n-m-e2-s1b-02.s.s1.r.b: If you do not know the length of the objects, you cannot know the total length either.
n-m-e2-s1b-02.s.s1.o.c: Lay one object of known length end to end in the same way and count how many times.
n-m-e2-s1b-02.s.s1.o.d: Count only the number of times, without matching the length of the objects.
n-m-e2-s1b-02.s.s1.r.d: The number of times alone does not tell you the length. You need to know the length of one object so you can multiply it by the number of times.
n-m-e2-s1b-02.s.s1.explain: If you use one object of known length as the reference and count how many times you laid it, you can estimate the total length as "length of one × number of times."
n-m-e2-s1b-02.s.s2.prompt: Let the length of one object be a cm and the number of times laid end to end be n. Make three different objects that, when laid end to end, make a length close to 100 cm (from 95 cm to 105 cm). The object is from 10 cm to 50 cm, and the number of times is from 2 to 10.
n-m-e2-s1b-02.s.s2.hint.0: Choose a length for one object, and add it up to see how many times you need to add it to get close to 100.
n-m-e2-s1b-02.s.s2.hint.1: If the total is less than 95 or more than 105, increase or decrease the number of times and try again.
n-m-e2-s1b-02.s.s2.var.n: Number of times laid end to end n (times)
n-m-e2-s1b-02.s.s2.ok.c1: The length of the object is between 10 cm and 50 cm.
n-m-e2-s1b-02.s.s2.fail.c1: Please choose a from the whole numbers between 10 and 50.
n-m-e2-s1b-02.s.s2.ok.c2: The number of times is between 2 and 10.
n-m-e2-s1b-02.s.s2.fail.c2: Please choose n from the whole numbers between 2 and 10.
n-m-e2-s1b-02.s.s2.ok.c3: The total length laid end to end is close to 100 cm.
n-m-e2-s1b-02.s.s2.fail.c3: Choose again so that a times n is between 95 cm and 105 cm.
n-m-e2-s1b-02.s.s2.explain: You can multiply the length of one by the number of times to get close to 100, like 10 cm 10 times, 20 cm 5 times, 25 cm 4 times, or 50 cm 2 times. It does not have to be exactly 100, like 33 cm 3 times (99 cm); being close is fine for an estimate.
n-m-e2-s1b-02.s.s3.prompt: You laid a 25 cm notebook end to end 4 times, but small gaps appeared between the notebooks. How is the real length from the left end of the first notebook to the right end of the last notebook compared with 100 cm?
n-m-e2-s1b-02.s.s3.hint.0: Draw two notebooks with a gap between them, and look at what is included from the left end to the right end.
n-m-e2-s1b-02.s.s3.hint.1: Put the length with no gaps and the length with gaps side by side and compare which is longer.
n-m-e2-s1b-02.s.s3.r.a: A gap is an empty place, so it does not make the length shorter; it makes it longer. Draw one gap and look at how far it extends.
n-m-e2-s1b-02.s.s3.o.c: It is exactly the same as 100 cm.
n-m-e2-s1b-02.s.s3.r.c: You only added the lengths of the 4 notebooks. The empty places between the notebooks are also part of the length from start to end.
n-m-e2-s1b-02.s.s3.o.d: You have to know how big the gaps are to say longer or shorter.
n-m-e2-s1b-02.s.s3.r.d: Even if you do not know how big the gaps are, if there are gaps, you know which way it grows. You can tell the direction even without knowing the amount.
n-m-e2-s1b-02.s.s3.explain: Adding only the 4 notebooks gives 100 cm, and the gaps between the notebooks also count toward the length from start to end. So the real length is longer than 100 cm. When laying objects end to end, place them tightly with no gaps so the estimate is accurate.

n-m-e2-s1b-03.title: Guessing Minseo's Secret Rule
n-m-e2-s1b-03.topic: Sorting: Guessing the Sorting Rule and Counting the Sorted Items
n-m-e2-s1b-03.goal: Learners see that when only a few cards are shown, more than one rule can fit; they pick the card that tells two rules apart, and check that the counts of the sorted groups must add up to the total.
n-m-e2-s1b-03.material: Minseo sorted shape cards into boxes "Ga" and "Na". She did not say what rule she used to sort them. The cards differ in shape (triangle, circle), color (red, blue), and size (big, small). Look at the cards and guess Minseo's rule.
n-m-e2-s1b-03.thinking.0: Knowing that more than one rule can fit the examples you see
n-m-e2-s1b-03.thinking.1: Choosing an example that tells two ideas apart, and testing it
n-m-e2-s1b-03.thinking.2: Checking that the counts after sorting add up to the total
n-m-e2-s1b-03.prereq.0: Telling apart by shape name (triangle, circle), color, and size
n-m-e2-s1b-03.prereq.1: Sorting by a rule and counting
n-m-e2-s1b-03.s.s1.prompt: Choose how your thinking changes each time a card is shown.
n-m-e2-s1b-03.s.s1.hint.0: Write down the cards by box, and look at color, shape, and size one at a time.
n-m-e2-s1b-03.s.s1.hint.1: Sort by the rule you chose and check one by one that all the cards shown so far go into the right boxes.
n-m-e2-s1b-03.s.s1.st.0.info: Box Ga: big red triangle, big blue triangle. Box Na: small red circle, small blue circle.
n-m-e2-s1b-03.s.s1.st.0.after: By shape or by size, the four cards are divided the same way. So it is still hard to decide on just one. It is not color.
n-m-e2-s1b-03.s.s1.st.0.r.a: Both boxes have a mix of red and blue, so it is not sorted by color.
n-m-e2-s1b-03.s.s1.st.0.r.b: It fits all four cards. But you need to check whether other rules fit too.
n-m-e2-s1b-03.s.s1.st.0.r.c: It fits all four cards. But you need to check whether other rules fit too.
n-m-e2-s1b-03.s.s1.st.0.o.d: You cannot decide on just one with the cards now.
n-m-e2-s1b-03.s.s1.st.0.r.d: This thinking sees that more than one rule might fit.
n-m-e2-s1b-03.s.s1.st.1.info: Minseo said, "I will show you one card that can tell shape and size apart. Which card would be good?"
n-m-e2-s1b-03.s.s1.st.1.ask: Which card can tell the two ideas apart?
n-m-e2-s1b-03.s.s1.st.1.after: A card whose shape and size do not go together (a big circle or a small triangle) can tell the two ideas apart. A card that ends up in the same box either way does not help.
n-m-e2-s1b-03.s.s1.st.1.r.a: This card goes in Box Ga whether you sort by shape or by size. Both ideas give the same answer, so it cannot tell them apart.
n-m-e2-s1b-03.s.s1.st.1.r.b: By shape it goes in Box Ga, and by size it goes in Box Na, so the two ideas give different answers.
n-m-e2-s1b-03.s.s1.st.1.r.c: This card goes in Box Na whether you sort by shape or by size. Both ideas give the same answer, so it cannot tell them apart.
n-m-e2-s1b-03.s.s1.st.1.r.d: By shape it goes in Box Na, and by size it goes in Box Ga, so the two ideas give different answers.
n-m-e2-s1b-03.s.s1.st.2.info: This time Minseo showed the big red circle card herself. This card went into Box Ga.
n-m-e2-s1b-03.s.s1.st.2.after: The big circle went into Box Ga, so shape is not the rule. So far only size fits all the cards.
n-m-e2-s1b-03.s.s1.st.2.r.a: There are circles in Box Na too. A circle also went into Box Ga, so shape does not fit.
n-m-e2-s1b-03.s.s1.st.2.r.b: Box Ga has both red and blue, so it is not color.
n-m-e2-s1b-03.s.s1.st.2.r.c: All five cards seen so far fit size.
n-m-e2-s1b-03.s.s1.st.2.r.d: We can tell it is not shape and not color.
n-m-e2-s1b-03.s.s1.st.3.info: I think size is the rule. Minseo took out a small blue triangle card.
n-m-e2-s1b-03.s.s1.st.3.ask: Which box will this card go into?
n-m-e2-s1b-03.s.s1.st.3.after: Every small card goes into Box Na. If you know the rule, you can tell in advance which box a card you have not seen yet will go into.
n-m-e2-s1b-03.s.s1.st.3.o.a: Box Ga. Because it is a triangle.
n-m-e2-s1b-03.s.s1.st.3.r.a: That is the answer if you think shape is the rule. We just said shape is not the rule.
n-m-e2-s1b-03.s.s1.st.3.o.b: Box Na. Because it is a small card.
n-m-e2-s1b-03.s.s1.st.3.r.b: You used the idea that size is the rule to predict for the new card.
n-m-e2-s1b-03.s.s1.st.3.r.c: Every card has to go into one of the two boxes.
n-m-e2-s1b-03.s.s1.st.3.o.d: Both 가 and 나 are fine.
n-m-e2-s1b-03.s.s1.st.3.r.d: A good rule can't put the same card in 가 one day and in 나 another day.
n-m-e2-s1b-03.s.s1.reflect: The first four cards split the same way by shape and by size, so we couldn't settle on one rule. When we added a card that tells the two ideas apart, only one was left. Talk about this: when there are few cards, more than one rule can fit, and you can choose a card that tells the rules apart and test with it.
n-m-e2-s1b-03.s.s2.prompt: After sorting all the cards, we counted 5 cards in box 가 and 4 cards in box 나. There were 8 cards in all. Choose everything you should check.
n-m-e2-s1b-03.s.s2.hint.0: Add the numbers in box 가 and box 나 and compare with the total of 8 cards.
n-m-e2-s1b-03.s.s2.hint.1: Think about whether each card goes into only one box, and recount the cards box by box, pointing to them one at a time.
n-m-e2-s1b-03.s.s2.o.a: Trust only the 5 cards in box 가 and don't recount the rest.
n-m-e2-s1b-03.s.s2.r.a: The sum is not 8. If you trust only one box, you can't find where the mistake is.
n-m-e2-s1b-03.s.s2.o.b: Recount to check whether one card was counted in both boxes.
n-m-e2-s1b-03.s.s2.o.c: Recount to check whether the number of cards at the start really was 8.
n-m-e2-s1b-03.s.s2.o.d: Secretly take one card out of box 나 so the sum becomes 8.
n-m-e2-s1b-03.s.s2.r.d: If you force the numbers to match, you can't tell where the mistake was. You have to find where it went wrong.
n-m-e2-s1b-03.s.s2.explain: One card goes into only one box, so the numbers in the boxes should add up to the total. If 5+4=9 but there are 8 cards in all, you may have counted one card twice or miscounted the cards at the start. You need to check both.

n-m-e2-s1b-03.s.s3.hint.1: If both ways give the same result, think about which card you could look at next to make them different.

n-m-e2-s1b-03.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you write it so a friend could read it and understand?

n-m-e2-s1b-03.s.s3.model.1: With only four cards, both the shape rule and the size rule fit. If we add a card that tells them apart, we can find out.
n-m-e2-s1b-03.s.s3.model.2: It's hard to settle on one. It could be shape or size, so I need to look at one more new card before deciding.

n-m-e2-s1b-04.title: How many times as many are the red marbles and the blue marbles?
n-m-e2-s1b-04.topic: Multiplication: how many times as many (which one is the base)
n-m-e2-s1b-04.goal: Understand that in 'A is how many times B', the base side (B) is seen as one group and you count how many groups there are, and explain to a younger sibling in easy words why saying it the other way around is wrong.
n-m-e2-s1b-04.material: Yeonseo has 12 red marbles and 4 blue marbles. Yeonseo wants to describe the two numbers of marbles using the words 'how many times'. Her younger sibling Hayun still finds 'how many times' hard. Yeonseo will use grouping to teach her.
n-m-e2-s1b-04.thinking.0: Finding the base side in 'how many times'
n-m-e2-s1b-04.thinking.1: Knowing when saying it the other way around changes the meaning
n-m-e2-s1b-04.thinking.2: Making number pairs that fit a condition
n-m-e2-s1b-04.prereq.0: Counting in groups of the same number
n-m-e2-s1b-04.prereq.1: Meaning of 'how many times' (how many groups of one group)
n-m-e2-s1b-04.s.s1.prompt: Choose the right statement about Yeonseo's marbles.
n-m-e2-s1b-04.s.s1.hint.0: Treat the 4 blue marbles as one group, and group the 12 red marbles by 4s.
n-m-e2-s1b-04.s.s1.hint.1: Count how many groups there are, and check again which side you treated as one group.
n-m-e2-s1b-04.s.s1.o.a: The red marbles are 4 times the blue marbles.
n-m-e2-s1b-04.s.s1.r.a: 4 is the number of blue marbles, not the number of groups. Count how many groups you get when you group by 4s.
n-m-e2-s1b-04.s.s1.o.b: The blue marbles are 3 times the red marbles.
n-m-e2-s1b-04.s.s1.r.b: You said it the other way around. The side that is 3 times is the side with more. Treat 4 as one group and look at how many groups 12 makes.
n-m-e2-s1b-04.s.s1.o.c: The red marbles are 3 times the blue marbles.
n-m-e2-s1b-04.s.s1.o.d: The red marbles are 8 times the blue marbles.
n-m-e2-s1b-04.s.s1.r.d: You read 12 minus 4 as the number of times. We don't find 'times' by subtracting; we find it by counting groups of the same number.
n-m-e2-s1b-04.s.s1.explain: If you treat the 4 blue marbles as one group, the 12 red marbles are 3 groups of 4. So the red marbles are 3 times the blue marbles. The blue marbles are not 3 times the red marbles.
n-m-e2-s1b-04.s.s2.prompt: This time, let's make our own marbles. Make three different pairs where a red marbles are 3 times b blue marbles. The blue marbles are from 2 to 10.
n-m-e2-s1b-04.s.s2.hint.0: Pick a number of blue marbles, then add that number 3 times.
n-m-e2-s1b-04.s.s2.hint.1: Check whether the sum is the number of red marbles, and the other way around, whether grouping the red marbles by the number of blue marbles gives 3 groups.
n-m-e2-s1b-04.s.s2.ok.c1: The number of blue marbles is between 2 and 10.
n-m-e2-s1b-04.s.s2.fail.c1: Please make b a natural number from 2 to 10.
n-m-e2-s1b-04.s.s2.ok.c2: The number of red marbles is a natural number.
n-m-e2-s1b-04.s.s2.fail.c2: Please make a a natural number.
n-m-e2-s1b-04.s.s2.ok.c3: The number of red marbles is 3 times the number of blue marbles.
n-m-e2-s1b-04.s.s2.fail.c3: The red marbles are not 3 times the blue marbles. Treat b blue marbles as one group and count how many groups there are.
n-m-e2-s1b-04.s.s2.explain: The number of red marbles is the number you get by making 3 groups of b blue marbles. When b=2 it is 6, when b=3 it is 9, when b=5 it is 15, and so on, so you can make pairs. If you write a and b the other way around, it is not 3 times but 1/3 as many.
n-m-e2-s1b-04.s.s3.prompt: Explain in easy words to Hayun why the statement 'the red marbles are 3 times the blue marbles' is right. Also write why it is wrong to say 'the blue marbles are 3 times the red marbles'.
n-m-e2-s1b-04.s.s3.hint.0: Put 4 blue marbles in one row, then line up the 12 red marbles in rows of 4.
n-m-e2-s1b-04.s.s3.hint.1: Count how many rows there are, and say which of the blue marbles and the red marbles is the base for the group.
n-m-e2-s1b-04.s.s3.placeholder: e.g. If we make 4 blue marbles one group, ...
n-m-e2-s1b-04.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you write that grouping by 4 blue marbles gives 3 groups?
n-m-e2-s1b-04.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you write which side is the base (one group)?
n-m-e2-s1b-04.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you write it in words Hayun can easily understand?
n-m-e2-s1b-04.s.s3.model.0: If we make 4 blue marbles one group, the 12 red marbles are 3 groups of 4. So the red marbles are 3 times the blue marbles. The blue marbles are fewer than the red marbles, so we must not say it the other way around as 3 times.
n-m-e2-s1b-04.s.s3.model.1: If we group by 4s, the red marbles make three groups. The side that becomes one group is the blue marbles. So the red marbles are 3 times the blue marbles, and saying the blue are 3 times the red is saying it the other way around.
n-m-e2-s1b-04.s.s3.model.2: If we group the 12 red marbles by 4, the number of the blue marbles, we get 3 groups. That's why it's 3 times. For the blue marbles to be 3 times, there would have to be 4 red marbles, and that's not the case.
n-m-e2-s1b-04.s.s3.model.3: If we make 4 blue marbles one group, the 12 red marbles are 3 groups, so it is 3 times. If the blue marbles were 3 times the red marbles, there would have to be 36 blue marbles, so we must not say it the other way around.

n-m-e2-s1b-05.title: Different ways to count stickers in groups
n-m-e2-s1b-05.topic: Multiplication: counting in groups and leftover singles
n-m-e2-s1b-05.goal: Check, by making several groupings, that after counting in groups of the same number you can find the total by adding the leftover singles without missing them, and that the total stays the same even when the group size changes.
n-m-e2-s1b-05.material: Jiho's collected stickers are scattered on the desk. Counting one by one is hard, so he decided to count in groups of the same number and set aside the leftover single stickers that aren't in a group. Jiho wants to try several ways of counting many stickers at a time.
n-m-e2-s1b-05.thinking.0: Finding the total by adding the number of groups and the singles together
n-m-e2-s1b-05.thinking.1: Showing the same total with different groupings
n-m-e2-s1b-05.thinking.2: Explaining why the number of groups gets smaller when the group size gets bigger
n-m-e2-s1b-05.s.s1.prompt: Jiho grouped the stickers by 5 and got 7 groups with 2 single stickers left over. How many stickers are there in all?
n-m-e2-s1b-05.s.s1.hint.0: First find how many stickers 7 groups of 5 make.
n-m-e2-s1b-05.s.s1.hint.1: Write the calculation each choice did as an expression, and compare it with the value you found yourself.
n-m-e2-s1b-05.s.s1.o.a: It's 35 stickers, because it's 7 groups of 5.
n-m-e2-s1b-05.s.s1.r.a: You left out the 2 single stickers. The leftover single stickers are stickers too.
n-m-e2-s1b-05.s.s1.o.b: It's 37 stickers. Add the 2 single stickers to 35.
n-m-e2-s1b-05.s.s1.o.c: It's 70 stickers. Multiply 5, 7 and 2 all together.
n-m-e2-s1b-05.s.s1.r.c: The 2 single stickers are a number to add, not to multiply.
n-m-e2-s1b-05.s.s1.o.d: It's 14 stickers. Add 5, 7 and 2 all together.
n-m-e2-s1b-05.s.s1.r.d: You just added instead of multiplying the number of groups by the number of stickers in a group. 7 groups of 5 is 5 added 7 times.
n-m-e2-s1b-05.s.s1.explain: 7 groups of 5 stickers is 5×7=35 stickers, and adding the 2 single stickers makes 37 stickers in all. You have to add the number counted in groups and the leftover singles together.
n-m-e2-s1b-05.s.s2.prompt: There are 37 stickers in all. Choose the number of stickers in a group g, the number of groups k, and the leftover single stickers r to make three different ways to get 37 stickers. A group has from 2 to 10 stickers. The leftover singles must be fewer than the number of stickers in a group.
n-m-e2-s1b-05.s.s2.hint.0: Choose the number of stickers in a group, then count how many groups you get by grouping by that number, using the multiplication table or adding.
n-m-e2-s1b-05.s.s2.hint.1: Subtract all the stickers in the groups from 37, and check whether the leftover singles are fewer than the number of stickers in a group.
n-m-e2-s1b-05.s.s2.ok.c1: A group has between 2 and 10 stickers.
n-m-e2-s1b-05.s.s2.fail.c1: Please make g a natural number from 2 to 10.
n-m-e2-s1b-05.s.s2.ok.c2: The number of groups is a natural number.
n-m-e2-s1b-05.s.s2.fail.c2: Please make k a natural number that is 1 or more.
n-m-e2-s1b-05.s.s2.ok.c3: The leftover singles are 0 or more and fewer than the number of stickers in a group.
n-m-e2-s1b-05.s.s2.fail.c3: Please make r a number that is 0 or more and less than g. If there are g or more singles, you can make one more group.
n-m-e2-s1b-05.s.s2.ok.c4: Adding up the stickers in the groups and the singles gives 37.
n-m-e2-s1b-05.s.s2.fail.c4: k groups of g stickers plus r single stickers does not make 37. Calculate again.
n-m-e2-s1b-05.s.s2.explain: There are many ways: when g is 2, 18 groups and 1 sticker; when 3, 12 groups and 1 sticker; when 4, 9 groups and 1 sticker; when 5, 7 groups and 2 stickers. Even if the way of grouping is different, the total of 37 stickers doesn't change.
n-m-e2-s1b-05.s.s3.prompt: Grouping by 5 gives 7 groups with 2 singles left over, and grouping by 10 gives 3 groups with 7 singles left over. Write why the number of groups changes but there are still exactly 37 stickers.
n-m-e2-s1b-05.s.s3.hint.0: Find how many stickers there are in the 7 groups of 5 and in the 3 groups of 10, each added to its singles.
n-m-e2-s1b-05.s.s3.hint.1: Put the number of stickers in a group and the number of groups for the two ways side by side and compare them.
n-m-e2-s1b-05.s.s3.placeholder: e.g. If we group by 10, each group has ...
n-m-e2-s1b-05.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you write that if the group size is different, the number of groups is different too?
n-m-e2-s1b-05.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you write that the total is the same once you add the singles?
n-m-e2-s1b-05.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you write it so the reader can easily understand?
n-m-e2-s1b-05.s.s3.model.0: If we group by 10, each group is bigger, so there are fewer groups. Even so, adding the singles gives 37 in all, the same.
n-m-e2-s1b-05.s.s3.model.1: If the number of stickers in a group is different, the number of groups is different. Groups of 5 make 7 groups with 2 left over, and groups of 10 make 3 groups with 7 left over, so either way the sum is 37 stickers.
n-m-e2-s1b-05.s.s3.model.2: If you put many in each group, there are fewer groups. If you add the leftover singles, the total number of stickers is the same.
n-m-e2-s1b-05.s.s3.model.3: Because the total number of stickers doesn't change; only the way of grouping changes.
n-m-e2-s1b-05.s.s3.model.4: Because there are singles left over. If there are fewer groups, there are more singles, so in the end it's the same.

n-m-e2-s2-01.title: Where did Suji's skip counting change?
n-m-e2-s2-01.goal: Understand that when you skip count by 100s, the tens digit and the ones digit stay the same even when the thousands digit changes, and find and fix the first mistake in a wrong skip count.
n-m-e2-s2-01.material: Suji is skip counting by 100s starting from 2750. In a four-digit number, the leftmost digit is the thousands place and the next is the hundreds place. Read what Suji wrote.
n-m-e2-s2-01.thinking.1: Making an example that goes across a boundary (where the thousands digit changes)
n-m-e2-s2-01.thinking.2: Reasoning about what changes and what stays the same in each place
n-m-e2-s2-01.prereq.0: Reading a four-digit number by thousands, hundreds, tens and ones places
n-m-e2-s2-01.prereq.1: Skip counting by 100s (the hundreds digit goes up by 1)
n-m-e2-s2-01.s.s1.prompt: Choose the one line where Suji's skip counting first goes wrong.
n-m-e2-s2-01.s.s1.hint.0: For each line, write the number before and the number after side by side, and compare place by place to see which digit changed.
n-m-e2-s2-01.s.s1.hint.1: Think about how much the number really grows when you skip count by 100s, and check whether the amount it grew in each line is 100.
n-m-e2-s2-01.s.s1.line.0: Skip count by 100s starting from 2750. When it grows by 100, the hundreds digit goes up by 1.
n-m-e2-s2-01.s.s1.line.2: After 2950 comes 3000. When the hundreds place becomes 10, the thousands digit goes up by 1.
n-m-e2-s2-01.s.s1.explain: Lines 1 and 2 are right. In line 3, it is right that the thousands digit goes up by 1 and the hundreds digit becomes 0, but the 5 in the tens place disappeared. It should grow by only 100, so after 2950 comes 3050. Line 4 is wrong because it carries on the wrong value from line 3.
n-m-e2-s2-01.s.s2.prompt: Find starting numbers where the same thing happens as with Suji. Starting from a four-digit number a, the number after skip counting by 100 twice has the same thousands digit as a, and the number after three skip counts has a different thousands digit. Also, a must not be a number that is exactly divisible by 100. Make three different values of a.
n-m-e2-s2-01.s.s2.hint.0: Choose a starting number and write the numbers after skip counting by 100 three times, in order. See which skip count is the first one where the thousands digit changes.
n-m-e2-s2-01.s.s2.hint.1: For the thousands digit to change for the first time at the third skip count, test a few to see about what the hundreds digit of the starting number has to be.
n-m-e2-s2-01.s.s2.fail.c1: Please make a a natural number from 1000 to 9699.
n-m-e2-s2-01.s.s2.ok.c2: The tens place or the ones place of a has a digit that is not 0.
n-m-e2-s2-01.s.s2.fail.c2: a must be a number that is not divisible by 100.
n-m-e2-s2-01.s.s2.ok.c3: Up to the number after two skip counts by 100, the thousands digit is the same.
n-m-e2-s2-01.s.s2.fail.c3: The thousands digit has already changed at the number after two skip counts by 100.
n-m-e2-s2-01.s.s2.ok.c4: The thousands digit changes at the number after three skip counts by 100.
n-m-e2-s2-01.s.s2.fail.c4: The thousands digit is still the same at the number after three skip counts by 100.
n-m-e2-s2-01.s.s2.explain: For example, 4780 gives 4880, 4980, 5080. Even when the thousands digit changes, the 8 in the tens place stays. If the starting number has a ones digit left, that digit carries over even at the moment the thousands digit changes.
n-m-e2-s2-01.s.s3.prompt: When you skip count by 100s and the thousands digit changes, how should you write it?
n-m-e2-s2-01.s.s3.hint.0: Write side by side the numbers before and after the thousands digit changes for one of the starting numbers you just made.
n-m-e2-s2-01.s.s3.hint.1: Compare the two numbers place by place and mark which place changes and which stays the same.
n-m-e2-s2-01.s.s3.o.a: The thousands digit goes up by 1 and all the other places become 0
n-m-e2-s2-01.s.s3.r.a: This is the method Suji used. Write again what you really get when 2950 grows by 100.
n-m-e2-s2-01.s.s3.o.b: The thousands digit goes up by 1 and the hundreds digit stays the same
n-m-e2-s2-01.s.s3.r.b: Then it would grow by 1000 at once. Check whether that fits with skip counting by 100s.
n-m-e2-s2-01.s.s3.o.c: The thousands digit goes up by 1, only the hundreds digit becomes 0, and the rest stay the same
n-m-e2-s2-01.s.s3.r.c: This idea changes only as much as the 100s that gather into 1000, and leaves the lower places alone.
n-m-e2-s2-01.s.s3.o.d: The thousands digit stays the same and only the hundreds digit is written as 10
n-m-e2-s2-01.s.s3.r.d: Only one digit can be written in one place. Think about where the 10 hundreds go.
n-m-e2-s2-01.s.s3.explain: 10 groups of 100 make 1000. When the hundreds place becomes 10, the thousands digit goes up by 1 and the hundreds digit becomes 0. The tens and ones digits aren't touched while adding 100, so they stay the same. That's why after 2950 comes 3050.

n-m-e2-s2-02.title: Can we trust the multiplication table rule Mina found?
n-m-e2-s2-02.topic: Multiplication table: finding rules in the multiplication table
n-m-e2-s2-02.goal: Understand that a rule is not always true just because a few examples fit, and make your own expressions where an odd-number table's product is even, then explain why the product is even.
n-m-e2-s2-02.material: Mina was looking at the multiplication table and said this. "The 3s, 5s, 7s and 9s tables are the odd tables. The products are all odd, like 3×3=9, 3×5=15, 5×7=35, 7×9=63. So the products of odd tables are always odd."
n-m-e2-s2-02.thinking.0: Judging whether a rule is always true even when several examples fit
n-m-e2-s2-02.thinking.2: Finding the condition for a product to be even
n-m-e2-s2-02.s.s1.prompt: Choose all the expressions that show Mina's statement is not true.
n-m-e2-s2-02.s.s1.hint.0: For each expression, calculate the product and write whether it is even or odd.
n-m-e2-s2-02.s.s1.hint.1: Mina said 'always odd', so think about what kind of expression gives a result that goes against that statement.
n-m-e2-s2-02.s.s1.r.a: This is the 5s table and the product is 30, which is even. Look at whether an odd table can give a product that is not odd.
n-m-e2-s2-02.s.s1.r.b: The product is odd, so it agrees with Mina's statement. Even if there are more examples that fit, that doesn't mean the statement is always true.
n-m-e2-s2-02.s.s1.r.c: The product is odd, so it agrees with Mina's statement. Collecting more examples that fit is different from finding a wrong example.
n-m-e2-s2-02.s.s1.r.d: This is the 3s table and the product is 24, which is even. Look at whether an odd table can give a product that is not odd.
n-m-e2-s2-02.s.s1.explain: 5×6=30 and 3×8=24 are examples where an odd table gives an even product. Even just one such example shows that Mina's statement is not always true. 7×7 and 9×3 are examples that agree with Mina's statement, so they don't show that the statement is wrong.
n-m-e2-s2-02.s.s2.prompt: Make three different expressions in the multiplication table where Mina's statement is not true. Multiply an odd table x (one of 3, 5, 7, 9) by a number y (from 2 to 9) so that the product is even.
n-m-e2-s2-02.s.s2.hint.0: Choose one odd table and write the products as you change the multiplier from 2 to 9 in order.
n-m-e2-s2-02.s.s2.hint.1: Mark separately the cells where the product is even and the cells where it is odd.
n-m-e2-s2-02.s.s2.ok.c2: y is a number from 2 to 9.
n-m-e2-s2-02.s.s2.fail.c2: Please make y a natural number from 2 to 9.
n-m-e2-s2-02.s.s2.fail.c3: The product is not even. Calculate the product and check whether it is even.
n-m-e2-s2-02.s.s2.explain: Even in an odd table, if you multiply by an even number the product is even. For example, 3×8=24, 5×6=30, 9×4=36. Even just one makes Mina's statement wrong.
n-m-e2-s2-02.s.s3.prompt: Why were the products in the expressions you just made even? Write it using one of your expressions as an example.
n-m-e2-s2-02.s.s3.hint.0: Choose one of the expressions you just made, write the table number and the multiplier separately, and write which one is odd and which one is even.
n-m-e2-s2-02.s.s3.hint.1: Put side by side the expressions whose products came out even and the expressions that stayed odd (e.g. 3×5), and compare the multipliers.
n-m-e2-s2-02.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Is the product of the expression I used calculated correctly?
n-m-e2-s2-02.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you say what the multiplier is, not just the 'odd table'?
n-m-e2-s2-02.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you think of other expressions where multiplying by an even number gives an even product?
n-m-e2-s2-02.s.s3.model.0: 5×6=30. The 5s table is an odd table, but the multiplier 6 is even, so the product is even.
n-m-e2-s2-02.s.s3.model.1: As in 3×8=24, if you multiply by an even number, the product is even even in an odd table. So Mina's statement is not always true.
n-m-e2-s2-02.s.s3.modelNote.1: I wrote 'if you multiply by an even number' instead of the words 'the multiplier'.
n-m-e2-s2-02.s.s3.model.2: 9×4=36 and 7×2=14. The multipliers 4 and 2 are even, so the products are even too.
n-m-e2-s2-02.s.s3.model.3: 3×4 is adding 3 4 times, and if you add an even number of times it pairs up evenly, so it is even.
n-m-e2-s2-02.s.s3.model.4: 7×6=42. The product is even because 6 is even.

n-m-e2-s2-03.title: The hallway measured with rods: how far can we say its length?
n-m-e2-s2-03.topic: Measuring length: m and cm, estimating
n-m-e2-s2-03.goal: Measure a length with several tools and say a range, 'between this and that', not 'exactly this', and understand that the smaller the unit you measure with, the narrower the range gets.
n-m-e2-s2-03.material: Seojin is measuring the length of the school hallway. One end of the hallway is a wall. Seojin doesn't find out the length all at once, but tells us the results measured with smaller and smaller tools, one at a time.
n-m-e2-s2-03.thinking.0: Improving an estimate with new information
n-m-e2-s2-03.prereq.1: Measuring length with a ruler or a rod
n-m-e2-s2-03.s.s1.prompt: Choose how it would be good to state the length of the hallway each time new information comes out.
n-m-e2-s2-03.s.s1.hint.0: At each step, draw how many times the rod or ruler was placed and what was left after that.
n-m-e2-s2-03.s.s1.hint.1: Compare 'the length that could be placed' and 'the length that went past' and think about whether the length of the hallway is in between.
n-m-e2-s2-03.s.s1.st.0.info: When the 1m rod was placed along the hallway to the end, it could be placed fully 3 times, and placing it a 4th time goes past the end of the hallway.
n-m-e2-s2-03.s.s1.st.0.ask: How should we state the length of the hallway?
n-m-e2-s2-03.s.s1.st.0.after: The hallway is longer than 3m and shorter than 4m. Even if we can't measure it exactly, we can say 'between this and that'.
n-m-e2-s2-03.s.s1.st.0.r.a: It was placed 3 times and didn't reach the end. Think about the part that was left over by the rod.
n-m-e2-s2-03.s.s1.st.0.r.b: This idea uses the information as it is: it could be placed 3 times and the 4th time went past.
n-m-e2-s2-03.s.s1.st.0.r.c: Placing the 4th rod goes past the end. Think about whether 4m is longer or shorter than the hallway.
n-m-e2-s2-03.s.s1.st.0.o.d: We can't say anything from what was measured with the rod
n-m-e2-s2-03.s.s1.st.0.r.d: Saying a range is also one way of knowing a length. Think again about what 3 rods and 4 rods mean.
n-m-e2-s2-03.s.s1.st.1.info: A 50cm rod was held against the remaining part, and it couldn't be placed fully even once. The 50cm rod is longer than the remaining part.
n-m-e2-s2-03.s.s1.st.1.ask: Now, how can we state the length of the hallway?
n-m-e2-s2-03.s.s1.st.1.after: The range got narrower, from between 3m and 4m to between 3m and 3m 50cm.
n-m-e2-s2-03.s.s1.st.1.r.a: The remaining part was shorter than the 50cm rod. Think about the length of 3m plus the remaining part.
n-m-e2-s2-03.s.s1.st.1.r.b: It was said that the 50cm rod was longer than the remaining part. Think about whether it was placed exactly.
n-m-e2-s2-03.s.s1.st.1.r.c: This idea narrows the range using the information that the 50cm rod went past the remaining part.
n-m-e2-s2-03.s.s1.st.1.o.d: Nothing has changed except that it is between 3m and 4m
n-m-e2-s2-03.s.s1.st.1.r.d: Look at whether the new information can make the range narrower.
n-m-e2-s2-03.s.s1.st.2.info: A 10cm ruler was placed on the remaining part, and it could be placed 3 times, with a little left after that. But there isn't enough room for a 4th.
n-m-e2-s2-03.s.s1.st.2.ask: Estimate the length of the hallway and say it.
n-m-e2-s2-03.s.s1.st.2.after: The range got narrower, to between 3m 30cm and 3m 40cm. You can pick one value inside it and estimate 'about this much'.
n-m-e2-s2-03.s.s1.st.2.r.a: This idea uses the information as it is: the 10cm ruler was placed 3 times with a little left.
n-m-e2-s2-03.s.s1.st.2.r.b: It was said that after placing the ruler 3 times there was a little left. Think about whether it could be exactly 30cm when there is a part left over.
n-m-e2-s2-03.s.s1.st.2.r.c: There wasn't enough room to place the 10cm ruler a 4th time. Compare with 3m 40cm.
n-m-e2-s2-03.s.s1.st.2.o.d: Estimate it as about 3m 35cm, between 3m 30cm and 3m 40cm
n-m-e2-s2-03.s.s1.st.2.r.d: This idea picks something near the middle of the range as the estimate. But it doesn't mean the real length is that value.
n-m-e2-s2-03.s.s1.st.3.info: Finally, it was measured with a tape measure with 1cm marks, and the length of the hallway was 3m 36cm.
n-m-e2-s2-03.s.s1.st.3.ask: If we show 3m 36cm using only cm, how much is it?
n-m-e2-s2-03.s.s1.st.3.r.a: 3m is 300cm. Check whether you changed 3m into 3000cm.
n-m-e2-s2-03.s.s1.st.3.r.c: This idea changes 3m into cm and adds 36cm.
n-m-e2-s2-03.s.s1.st.3.r.d: Check whether you read 36cm as 10 times as much, like 360cm.
n-m-e2-s2-03.s.s1.reflect: The smaller the tool got, the narrower the range in which we could state the length of the hallway became. At the start too, we said 'between this and that' instead of 'exactly this', so the first statement was not wrong when new information came. Talk about which statements changed and which stayed the same as the information grew.
n-m-e2-s2-03.s.s2.prompt: Now that you know the information from the 10cm ruler, say three different values the length of the hallway could be. Say the length in m and cm, with cm a number from 0 to 99.
n-m-e2-s2-03.s.s2.hint.0: Write in m and cm the 'place not yet passed' and the 'place passed' that you found in the first three steps.
n-m-e2-s2-03.s.s2.hint.1: Choose a few lengths between the two places, write them in m and cm, and check whether they fit the information from every step.
n-m-e2-s2-03.s.s2.ok.c1: m and cm are natural numbers in the proper range.
n-m-e2-s2-03.s.s2.fail.c1: Please make m a natural number from 0 to 9 and cm a natural number from 0 to 99.
n-m-e2-s2-03.s.s2.ok.c2: The 10cm ruler was placed 3 times and there was still some left, so it is longer than 3m 30cm.
n-m-e2-s2-03.s.s2.fail.c2: It has to be longer than 3m 30cm. The 10cm ruler was placed 3 times and a little was still left.
n-m-e2-s2-03.s.s2.ok.c3: There wasn't enough room to place the 10cm ruler 4 times, so it is shorter than 3m 40cm.
n-m-e2-s2-03.s.s2.fail.c3: It has to be shorter than 3m 40cm. There wasn't enough room to place the 10cm ruler a 4th time.
n-m-e2-s2-03.s.s2.explain: The place after placing the 10cm ruler 3 times is 3m 30cm, and after placing it 4 times it is 3m 40cm. The hallway is between them, so it can be any value from 3m 31cm to 3m 39cm.
n-m-e2-s2-03.s.s3.prompt: What changed each time Seojin measured with a smaller tool?
n-m-e2-s2-03.s.s3.hint.0: Write the range of the length stated at each step on its own line, and compare how many cm wide each range is.
n-m-e2-s2-03.s.s3.hint.1: Check whether what was said at the start fits the final result, and which statement changed.
n-m-e2-s2-03.s.s3.o.a: The hallway actually got longer and longer
n-m-e2-s2-03.s.s3.r.a: The length of the hallway did not change. Think about which statement changed.
n-m-e2-s2-03.s.s3.o.b: The range in which we can state the length of the hallway got narrower and narrower
n-m-e2-s2-03.s.s3.r.b: This points out that the smaller the tool you measure with, the narrower the width of 'between this and that' becomes.
n-m-e2-s2-03.s.s3.o.c: The statement at the start, between 3m and 4m, became a wrong statement
n-m-e2-s2-03.s.s3.r.c: The later result, 3m 36cm, is between 3m and 4m. Check whether the first statement was wrong.
n-m-e2-s2-03.s.s3.o.d: No matter which tool you measure with, how well you can know the length is the same
n-m-e2-s2-03.s.s3.r.d: Compare whether how much you can know is the same with the 1m rod and the 1cm tape measure.
n-m-e2-s2-03.s.s3.explain: The length of the hallway stays the same. With the 1m rod we can know it is between 3m and 4m, with the 10cm ruler between 3m 30cm and 3m 40cm, and with the 1cm tape measure down to 3m 36cm. The smaller the marks of the tool, the narrower the range.

n-m-e2-s2-04.title: How do we count the time slept past midnight?
n-m-e2-s2-04.topic: Time of day and time: finding the time that passes through the night
n-m-e2-s2-04.goal: When someone falls asleep in the afternoon and wakes up in the morning, split the time at midnight (12 at night) to find how long it took, and make your own pairs of bedtime and wake-up time with the same amount of sleep.
n-m-e2-s2-04.material: Haeun fell asleep at 9:30 p.m. In the morning she woke up at 6:30 a.m. A day is 24 hours, and at midnight a.m. and p.m. switch. We want to find out how many hours Haeun slept.
n-m-e2-s2-04.thinking.0: Finding the time by splitting it at midnight
n-m-e2-s2-04.thinking.1: Making several pairs that fit a condition
n-m-e2-s2-04.thinking.2: Finding the rule between the pairs
n-m-e2-s2-04.prereq.0: Reading the time in hours and minutes
n-m-e2-s2-04.s.s1.prompt: Choose the right way to find how long Haeun slept.
n-m-e2-s2-04.s.s1.hint.0: Draw two clocks to show the time she fell asleep and the time she woke up, and follow the clock hands as they pass midnight.
n-m-e2-s2-04.s.s1.hint.1: Split the time at midnight and find the first part and the second part separately.
n-m-e2-s2-04.s.s1.r.a: You subtracted only the numbers without telling p.m. and a.m. apart. Follow it on a clock to see whether this time matches the time she actually slept.
n-m-e2-s2-04.s.s1.o.b: Count only the 2 hours 30 minutes up to midnight to get 2 hours 30 minutes
n-m-e2-s2-04.s.s1.r.b: You left out the time she slept after midnight until she woke up in the morning.
n-m-e2-s2-04.s.s1.o.c: Add 9:30 and 6:30 to get 16 hours in all
n-m-e2-s2-04.s.s1.r.c: Adding two times of day has nothing to do with the time slept. Think about what it would mean to add times of day.
n-m-e2-s2-04.s.s1.o.d: Split at midnight and add 2 hours 30 minutes and 6 hours 30 minutes to get 9 hours
n-m-e2-s2-04.s.s1.r.d: This idea splits the time in two at midnight, finds each part, and adds them.
n-m-e2-s2-04.s.s1.explain: From 9:30 p.m. to midnight is 2 hours 30 minutes, and from midnight to 6:30 a.m. is 6 hours 30 minutes. Together that is 9 hours. It is easy if you split at midnight, where p.m. and a.m. switch.
n-m-e2-s2-04.s.s2.prompt: From some day on, Haeun decided to sleep exactly 9 hours. She falls asleep at exactly s p.m. and wakes up at exactly w a.m. s is a number from 6 to 11, and w is a number from 4 to 9. Make three different pairs (s, w).
n-m-e2-s2-04.s.s2.hint.0: Choose a bedtime and first write how many hours it is until midnight.
n-m-e2-s2-04.s.s2.hint.1: Subtract the time until midnight from 9 hours to get the time she must sleep after midnight. The time reached after that much time is the wake-up time.
n-m-e2-s2-04.s.s2.ok.c1: The bedtime is between 6 p.m. and 11 p.m.
n-m-e2-s2-04.s.s2.fail.c1: Please make s a natural number from 6 to 11.
n-m-e2-s2-04.s.s2.ok.c2: The wake-up time is between 4 a.m. and 9 a.m.
n-m-e2-s2-04.s.s2.fail.c2: Please make w a natural number from 4 to 9.
n-m-e2-s2-04.s.s2.ok.c3: The time slept is exactly 9 hours.
n-m-e2-s2-04.s.s2.fail.c3: The time slept is not 9 hours. Split it into the time up to midnight and the time after midnight and calculate again.
n-m-e2-s2-04.s.s2.explain: For example, if she falls asleep at 10 p.m. and wakes up at 7 a.m., it is 2 hours until midnight and 7 hours after, which makes 9 hours in all. 7 p.m. to 4 a.m. and 11 p.m. to 8 a.m. are also 9 hours.
n-m-e2-s2-04.s.s3.prompt: Line up the pairs you just made. To sleep 9 hours, what rule is there between the bedtime and the wake-up time?
n-m-e2-s2-04.s.s3.hint.0: Write the pairs you made in a line, starting with the earliest bedtime, and look at how the wake-up time changes.
n-m-e2-s2-04.s.s3.hint.1: Try two things yourself. Find the time slept when you make the bedtime 1 hour later and keep the wake-up time the same, and when you make both 1 hour later.
n-m-e2-s2-04.s.s3.o.a: The bedtime and the wake-up time added together are always the same number
n-m-e2-s2-04.s.s3.r.a: Add the two numbers in the pairs you made. Check whether the sums are the same.
n-m-e2-s2-04.s.s3.o.b: If the bedtime is 1 hour later, the wake-up time is also 1 hour later
n-m-e2-s2-04.s.s3.r.b: This idea is that to keep the time slept the same, the start and the end have to move together.
n-m-e2-s2-04.s.s3.o.c: The wake-up time is always the same no matter the bedtime
n-m-e2-s2-04.s.s3.r.c: Look at whether the wake-up times in the pairs you made are all the same.
n-m-e2-s2-04.s.s3.o.d: If the bedtime is 1 hour later, the wake-up time is 1 hour earlier
n-m-e2-s2-04.s.s3.r.d: Think about how the time slept would change if you make the bedtime later and the wake-up time earlier.
n-m-e2-s2-04.s.s3.explain: To sleep 9 hours, the gap between the bedtime and the wake-up time must always be the same. So if the bedtime is 1 hour later, the wake-up time is also 1 hour later.

n-m-e2-s2-05.title: How far can we trust what we found from two tables?
n-m-e2-s2-05.topic: Tables and graphs: what two tables can tell us
n-m-e2-s2-05.goal: Understand that two tables that survey the same people in two ways tell only each count separately and do not tell the number of people who chose both, and sort out what more data is needed to find that out.
n-m-e2-s2-05.material:
The 20 students of Class 1, Grade 2 were surveyed on two things. Each person chose only one fruit and one color. Everyone answered both surveys.
Favorite fruit: apple 9, tangerine 6, grape 5
Favorite color: red 8, blue 7, yellow 5
Jia looks at the two tables and wants to find out how many students like both red and apples.
n-m-e2-s2-05.thinking.0: Checking the totals of the tables
n-m-e2-s2-05.thinking.1: Telling apart what the two tables settle and what they do not settle
n-m-e2-s2-05.prereq.0: Organizing data in a table and finding the total
n-m-e2-s2-05.s.s1.prompt: Choose the one line in Jia's story where it first goes wrong.
n-m-e2-s2-05.s.s1.hint.0: For each line, sort out whether it was read straight from the table or whether it adds something that is not in the table.
n-m-e2-s2-05.s.s1.hint.1: Look for whether the table says which fruit the students who like red chose.
n-m-e2-s2-05.s.s1.line.0: The total of the fruit table is 9+6+5=20, so all 20 students in the class answered.
n-m-e2-s2-05.s.s1.line.1: The total of the color table is also 8+7+5=20, so the same 20 students all answered.
n-m-e2-s2-05.s.s1.line.2: The 8 students who like red are all among the 9 who like apples.
n-m-e2-s2-05.s.s1.line.3: So the number of students who like both red and apples is 8.
n-m-e2-s2-05.s.s1.explain: Lines 1 and 2 are right. The totals of both tables are 20, so the same 20 students answered. In line 3, saying the 8 red students are among the 9 apple students can't be known from the tables. The students who like red might like tangerines or grapes. Line 4 carries on the wrong idea from line 3.
n-m-e2-s2-05.s.s2.prompt: Decide which color each of the 9 students who chose apples chose. It must not go against the numbers in the two tables. Among the students who chose apples, x chose red, y chose blue, and z chose yellow. Make three different cases.
n-m-e2-s2-05.s.s2.hint.0: First check in the color table how many students there are for red, blue and yellow, and be careful not to put in more than that.
n-m-e2-s2-05.s.s2.hint.1: Choose x and split the remaining students between y and z.
n-m-e2-s2-05.s.s2.ok.c1: x, y and z are natural numbers that are 0 or more.
n-m-e2-s2-05.s.s2.fail.c1: Please make x, y and z natural numbers that are 0 or more.
n-m-e2-s2-05.s.s2.ok.c2: All 9 students who chose apples fall into one color each.
n-m-e2-s2-05.s.s2.fail.c2: Adding x, y and z must equal the number of students who chose apples.
n-m-e2-s2-05.s.s2.ok.c3: They are not more than the numbers in the color table (red 8, blue 7, yellow 5).
n-m-e2-s2-05.s.s2.fail.c3: It can't be more than the number of students of that color in the color table. Look at the color table again.
n-m-e2-s2-05.s.s2.explain: For example, (4, 3, 2) works and (8, 1, 0) works too. There are several cases that don't go against the numbers in the two tables, so the two tables alone can't tell us the number of students who like both red and apples.
n-m-e2-s2-05.s.s3.prompt: What more do we need to know how many students like both red and apples? Choose everything that would let us find out.
n-m-e2-s2-05.s.s3.hint.0: Look for what kind of data holds what the two tables don't have, that is, the information of one person choosing both things together.
n-m-e2-s2-05.s.s3.hint.1: For each choice, test whether knowing it would let you count on your fingers the people who like both red and apples.
n-m-e2-s2-05.s.s3.o.a: A table that writes each student's fruit and color together
n-m-e2-s2-05.s.s3.r.a: This idea is that the fruit and color a person chose must be paired up for us to count the people who chose both.
n-m-e2-s2-05.s.s3.o.b: Adding the totals of the two tables one more time
n-m-e2-s2-05.s.s3.r.b: We already found that the totals are the same, 20. Calculating the totals again tells us nothing new.
n-m-e2-s2-05.s.s3.o.c: The color each of the 9 students who chose apples picked
n-m-e2-s2-05.s.s3.r.c: If you look at the students who chose apples one by one, you can count how many chose red.
n-m-e2-s2-05.s.s3.o.d: Count again how many students are in the class in all
n-m-e2-s2-05.s.s3.r.d: You already knew the class has 20 students. It has nothing to do with how many students chose both things.
n-m-e2-s2-05.s.s3.explain: You need to match up the fruit and the color each person chose. It is enough to have a chart for each student, and if you know only the colors of the 9 students who chose apples, you get the number of red. Adding up the totals again or recounting the students is something you already know.
